source_text: Μηδεὶς ἐξαπατάτω ἑαυτόν; μήτε ὡς εὑρών, οὔτε γὰρ εὑρόντι κερδαίνειν ἔξεστι. Φησὶ γὰρ τὸ Δευτερονόμιον· Μὴ ἰδὼν τὸν μόσχον τοῦ ἀδελφοῦ σου καὶ τὸ πρόβατον πλανώμενα ἐν τῇ ὁδῷ ὑπερίδῃς αὐτά· ἀποστροφῇ ἀποστρέψεις αὐτὰ τῷ ἀδελφῷ σου. Ἐὰν δὲ μὴ ἐγγίζῃ ὁ ἀδελφός σου πρὸς σέ, μηδὲ ἐπίστασαι αὐτόν, συνάξεις αὐτὰ καὶ ἔσται μετὰ σοῦ, ἕως ἂν ἐκζητήσῃ αὐτὰ ὁ ἀδελφός σου καὶ ἀποδώσεις αὐτῷ. Καὶ οὕτω ποιήσεις τὸν ὄνον αὐτοῦ, καὶ οὕτω ποιήσεις τὸ ἱμάτιον αὐτοῦ, καὶ οὕτω ποιήσεις κατὰ πᾶσαν ἀπώλειαν τοῦ ἀδελφοῦ σου, ὅσα ἂν ἀπόληται παρ᾿ αὐτοῦ, καὶ εὑρήσῃς αὐτὰ. Ταῦτα τὸ Δευτερονόμιον. Ἐν δὴ τῇ Ἐξόδῳ, οὐ μόνον ἐὰν τὰ τοῦ ἀδελφοῦ τις εὕρῃ, ἀλλὰ καὶ τοῦ ἐχθροῦ· Ἀποστροφῇ, φησὶν, ἀποστρέψεις αὐτὰ εἰς τὸν οἶκον τοῦ κυρίου αὐτῶν. Εἰ δὲ ἐν εἰρήνῃ ῥᾳθυμοῦντος καὶ τρυφῶντος καὶ τῶν ἰδίων ἀμελοῦντος ἀδελφοῦ ἢ ἐχθροῦ κερδάναι οὐκ ἔξεσται, πόσῳ μᾶλλον δυστυχοῦντος καὶ πολεμίους φεύγοντος καὶ κατὰ ἀνάγκην τὰ ἴδια ἐγκαταλείποντος;
thought_title: Finders may not keep what others lost
orientation: Finding something gives no right to keep it: the Law commands that lost goods be returned even to an enemy, and still more to someone who fled from the invaders.
pass_a_gloss: Let no one deceive himself; nor as having found, for not even to a finder is it permitted to profit. For Deuteronomy says: Having seen the calf of your brother and the sheep wandering on the road, do not overlook them; with a returning you shall return them to your brother. If your brother does not draw near to you, nor do you know him, you shall gather them and it shall be with you until your brother seeks them out, and you shall give [them] back to him. And thus you shall do [with] his donkey, and thus [with] his garment, and thus with every loss of your brother, whatever is lost from him and you find them. These things Deuteronomy. And in Exodus, not only if someone finds the things of the brother, but also of the enemy: with a returning, it says, you shall return them to the house of their master. But if from a brother or enemy being idle in peace and living luxuriously and neglecting his own things it will not be permitted to gain, how much more [not] from one being unfortunate, fleeing enemies, and by necessity abandoning his own things?

choices.why: The print sets a question mark, but the sense is a command.

choices.english: nor plead that he found the goods
choices.why: The participle gives the excuse being refused; 'the goods' is supplied for English.
The Greek says 'how much more [is it forbidden]'; English idiom states the same point as 'how much less [may one profit]'.

bible_refs.note: Deuteronomy named by Gregory; LXX quoted (μόσχον ... πρόβατον ... ἀποστροφῇ ἀποστρέψεις)
an enemy's stray animal must be returned; Gregory's wording ('to the house of their owner') differs from the LXX as usually printed

pass_b_english: Let no one deceive himself, nor plead that he found the goods; for not even a finder may make a profit. For Deuteronomy says: “If you see your brother’s calf or his sheep straying on the road, do not ignore them; you shall surely bring them back to your brother. And if your brother is not near you, and you do not know him, you shall gather them in, and they shall stay with you until your brother looks for them, and you shall give them back to him. You shall do the same with his donkey, the same with his garment, and the same with anything your brother loses—whatever is lost by him and you find” (Deuteronomy 22:1–3). So says Deuteronomy. And in Exodus this holds not only when someone finds what belongs to his brother but also what belongs to his enemy: “You shall surely bring them back,” it says, “to the house of their owner” (Exodus 23:4).

If, then, it is not allowed to profit from a brother or an enemy who in time of peace is careless, living in comfort, and neglecting his own goods, how much less from one who is in misfortune, fleeing from enemies, and forced by necessity to abandon his own goods?
notes: Rubric left out (editorial). The print sets a Greek question mark after ἑαυτόν; the sense is a command and is rendered so. Μηδεὶς ἐξαπατάτω ἑαυτόν has the wording of 1 Corinthians 3:18, but it is a stock phrase and Gregory does not apply Paul's context; possible echo only, not cited. μήτε ὡς εὑρών rendered 'nor plead that he found the goods' ('the goods' supplied for English). Deuteronomy 22:1–3 LXX quoted. The Exodus line is named by Gregory and matches the content of Exodus 23:4 (an enemy's stray animal), but its wording ('to the house of their owner') differs from the LXX text as usually printed (ἀποστρέψας ἀποδώσεις αὐτῷ); cited as Exodus 23:4, English follows Gregory's wording. κυρίου αὐτῶν = their human owner, so lower-case. 'this holds' supplied for the Greek ellipsis. πόσῳ μᾶλλον ('how much more [is it forbidden]') rendered with the English idiom 'how much less'.
